label: Grown-up goes away for a while

what_happens.title: What happens when a grown-up goes away
goals: The grown-up goes away for a set number of days
Someone the child knows looks after them
The grown-up comes back on a known day
what_happens.parentSkill: Explain the trip in sleeps: 'I'm going for five sleeps for work. On the sixth day, I come home.'

who_is_there.title: Who looks after me
goals: A known grown-up looks after the child
The away grown-up stays in touch
who_is_there.parentSkill: Name exactly who will do school runs, meals and bedtime while you are away.

what_i_do.title: What I do while they are away
goals: Cross off the days on the calendar
Stay in touch: calls, drawings, a journal
what_i_do.parentSkill: Leave a small item, like a T-shirt or a recorded story, and set up a simple way to share news.

if_scared.title: If I miss them a lot
goals: Feelings can be sad, angry or worried
Calm tools: the calendar, a hug, the smell T-shirt, slow breaths
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the feeling and point to the plan: 'You miss Papa. Three more sleeps, then he's home.'

rehearsal.title: Let's get ready for the trip
goals: Plan how to stay in touch
Choose the goodbye ritual and the welcome-home plan
rehearsal.parentSkill: Make the countdown calendar together and record a bedtime story before you leave.

steps: The grown-up explains where they are going and for how long
Make a countdown calendar with the days away
Say a special goodbye before the trip
Stay home with another grown-up who looks after me
Call, video chat or send pictures, as agreed
Cross off each day on the calendar
Welcome the grown-up home with a hug
sensory: an empty chair at the table
the grown-up's voice on a phone or a video call
a T-shirt or pillow that smells like the grown-up
a big hug at the door
honestyNotes: Children may miss the grown-up a lot, feel angry or act out; never promise calls at exact times unless they are certain, and never promise the child will not feel sad. Use sleeps or days, not vague words like 'soon'. For deployments or long absences, let the parent decide how much detail to share.

questionButtons.text: How long will you be gone?
fallbackAnswer: [[GROWNUP]] will tell you how many sleeps.
We can count them on the countdown calendar.
Yes. [[GROWNUP]] will tell you the coming-home day.
We will cross off the days until then.
A grown-up you know and trust will look after you.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you who.
We will try to call or send messages when we can.
Sometimes a call is missed because of time or work, and that is okay.

questionButtons.text: Why do you have to go?
fallbackAnswer: [[GROWNUP]] will tell you the reason, maybe work or helping family.
Going away does not change how much [[GROWNUP]] loves you.

questionButtons.text: What if I miss you too much?
fallbackAnswer: Missing someone is normal and shows how much you love them.
You can hug the special T-shirt and look at the calendar.
[[GROWNUP]] will be careful and tell you about the trip.
You can ask any question.
The grown-up at home will do your bedtime steps.
You can listen to a recorded story too.
Missing someone can feel cross or grumpy, not only sad.
Telling the grown-up at home helps.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you.
The best present is the welcome-home hug.

questionButtons.text: Why is it night there when it is day here?
fallbackAnswer: The world is round, and the sun shines on different places at different times.
That is why calls can be at funny times.

sentences.text: Soon one of [[CHILD]]'s grown-ups will go away for a while.
It might be for work, to help family, or for another reason.
The grown-up will tell [[CHILD]] how many sleeps it lasts.
A countdown calendar shows each day.
Before bed, here is a story about a young penguin called Pip.
Pip's papa had to swim far away to the fishing grounds for work.
I will be gone for five sleeps, he said.
On the sixth day, I will swim home.
They made an ice calendar with five little snowflakes.
While Papa was away, Mama and Grandma looked after Pip.
Every evening, Pip crossed off one snowflake.
Some evenings, Papa sent a message with a seagull.
On the fifth night, there was just one snowflake left.
In the morning, Papa waddled out of the sea, and Pip ran to hug him.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
While the grown-up is away, another grown-up [[CHILD]] knows will look after [[CHILD]].
The routines stay mostly the same: school, meals and bedtime.
There may be calls, video chats or pictures.
Last, on the coming-home day, there is a big hug.

He felt sad and cross at the same time.

Grown-ups travel for work, for training, to care for relatives, or for military service.
Knowing exactly how long and where helps the waiting feel more manageable.
Time zones can make calls tricky, so plans may change.
Families often find new routines while someone is away, which can be fun too.
[[CHILD]] can look at a map of where the grown-up is going.
Kids sometimes feel extra responsible while a parent is away, but taking care of the household is the grown-ups' job.
Military families and families with travelling parents often have support groups and resources.
Letting the school know helps teachers spot when a kid needs extra support.
It is normal to feel closer to the at-home grown-up and also to feel frustrated with them.
[[CHILD]] can keep a list of news to share on calls.
Keeping a shared photo album or a journal makes it easier to catch up.
Planning a special activity for the at-home days helps time pass.
Writing letters or emails can be a nice change from calls.
It is okay to have days when you do not feel like talking on the phone.
[[CHILD]] can be in charge of the countdown and announcing how many sleeps are left.
Missing someone often shows up as grumpiness or trouble sleeping, not only as sadness.
Worries about safety, especially with long trips or deployments, are normal, and asking questions helps.
Keeping a worry journal or talking to the at-home grown-up gives worries somewhere to go.
The reunion can feel strange too, as everyone gets used to being together again.
[[CHILD]] can plan the welcome-home moment.
Talking openly before the trip about feelings and plans makes the goodbye smoother.
Shared activities, like reading the same book in two places, keep a connection.
Agreeing on a call schedule, with a backup if it fails, avoids disappointment.
Planning a reunion activity gives the waiting a goal.
[[CHILD]] can choose a small item for the grown-up to take on the trip.
